title: The voyage that changed biology
text: When HMS Beagle sailed from Plymouth in December 1831, her captain wanted chiefly a gentleman companion for a long surveying voyage. The twenty-two-year-old he took aboard would instead {{1}} (REVOLUTION) the study of life itself. Charles Darwin collected {{2}} (FEVER) throughout the five-year journey: beetles in Argentina, fossils of extinct giants in Patagonia, finches and giant tortoises in the Galapagos. Yet the decisive clues were not the famous birds but the {{3}} (GEOLOGY) evidence — strata raised far above the sea, and fossils showing that species had vanished. Gradually Darwin concluded that the Earth was immensely old and that its surface, far from being fixed, was {{4}} (CEASE) remaking itself. Back in England, he then did something almost unbelievable: for nearly twenty years he delayed publication, assembling evidence and quietly dreading the {{5}} (REACT) his ideas would provoke. Only a letter from Alfred Russel Wallace, who had reached strikingly similar conclusions in Indonesia, forced his hand, and the two men's papers were presented together in 1858 — an act of {{6}} (COURTEOUS) that science rarely manages today. On the Origin of Species sold out on its first day, and its patient, devastating argument remains a {{7}} (REMARK) achievement — defended at Oxford in his absence by allies while its {{8}} (CARE) cautious author stayed quietly at home.

gaps.explanation: 'would revolutionise the study of life' — verb from revolution (British spelling).
'an act of courtesy' — noun from courteous.
'remains a remarkable achievement' — adjective from remark.
'its carefully cautious author' — adverb from care.
